cues.text: Hey, welcome back.
A coil creates a magnetic field, but place a material inside it and the
material can respond too.
Today's question is not just how strong the source is.
It is how matter changes the result.
Magnetisation, capital M, means net magnetic dipole moment per unit volume.
If microscopic moments cancel, the net magnetisation can be zero even though
individual moments exist.
Both magnetisation and magnetic field intensity, capital H, are measured in
amperes per meter.
The magnetic field B is measured in tesla.
In SI units, B equals mu zero times the sum of H and M.
For a linear isotropic material, M equals susceptibility chi times H.
Isotropic means the response has no preferred material direction.
Susceptibility has no units.
Combine those two equations and B equals mu zero times one plus chi times H.
Relative permeability is therefore one plus chi in this model.
Try this: chi is zero point zero zero two, and internal H is five hundred
amperes per meter.
What is M?
Take a moment.
It is one ampere per meter, aligned with H.
Relative permeability is one point zero zero two.
Notice we used internal H.
A specimen's shape can make internal H different from the field applied
without
the specimen.
For our numerical examples, internal H is given.
Keep that assumption visible; it saves a sneaky substitution error.
Imagine pointing H to the right.
In a diamagnetic material, the induced magnetisation points left.
That opposing response is encoded by negative susceptibility.
It does not mean every magnetic field inside the sample reverses direction.
The response is usually tiny, so B normally remains in the direction of H,
just
slightly reduced compared with mu zero H.
On the board, the orange arrow shows the response, not the total field.
Microscopically, the applied field changes the motion of electrons and induces
an opposing magnetic contribution.
This contribution exists widely, but a stronger paramagnetic or ferromagnetic
response can dominate the observed behaviour.
Familiar diamagnetic examples include bismuth, copper and water.
In a nonuniform external field, an ordinary weak diamagnetic sample tends
toward regions of weaker field.
In a uniform field, there is no such net translation from a field gradient.
Now calculate: chi is minus four times ten to the minus five, and internal H
is
two thousand amperes per meter to the right.
M is minus zero point zero eight amperes per meter.
The minus sign tells us left.
Relative permeability is zero point nine nine nine nine six, a little below
one, not negative.
For ordinary diamagnetic materials, susceptibility is approximately
independent
of temperature over the usual elementary model range.
JEE comparisons often test the sign, direction and temperature trend together.
Learn that connected picture, rather than three disconnected labels.
Now suppose atoms have permanent magnetic moments, but their directions are
disordered when no field is applied.
In a paramagnet, the field biases these moments toward alignment.
Thermal agitation keeps the alignment incomplete.
The result is a small positive susceptibility and magnetisation along H.
Aluminium and oxygen are useful elementary examples.
In a field gradient, a weak paramagnetic sample tends toward stronger field.
Again, that statement needs a nonuniform field; attraction is not a substitute
for checking geometry.
The ordinary response does not leave a stable permanent magnet when the field
is removed.
Temperature gives us a lovely competition: more thermal agitation makes
alignment harder.
For a material in the Curie law regime, susceptibility equals Curie constant C
divided by absolute temperature T.
Use kelvin, not degrees Celsius.
This is a model for appropriate materials and conditions, not a universal law
for every paramagnet.
Let's practise.
Susceptibility is zero point zero zero three at three hundred kelvin.
At six hundred kelvin, what should it be under this model?
Pause before dividing.
It becomes zero point zero zero one five.
At fixed internal H of eight hundred amperes per meter, magnetisation drops
from two point four to one point two amperes per meter.
The field did not become weaker; thermal disorder changed the material's
response.
If temperature is given in Celsius, convert first.
Ratios of Celsius temperatures do not preserve the Curie relation.
Iron can respond much more strongly than aluminium.
The difference is not simply that we turned up the same weak alignment
process.
In a ferromagnet, interactions favour cooperative ordering of neighbouring
microscopic moments.
Below the appropriate transition temperature, regions called domains can have
spontaneous magnetisation.
But a whole specimen need not start with a large net moment.
Different domains can point in different directions and largely cancel.
Look at the left hand sketch.
The arrows represent different domains, not single electrons.
Apply a field and favourable domains can grow; magnetisation can also rotate
toward the field.
The right hand sketch shows a stronger net alignment.
The response is generally nonlinear and depends on magnetic history.
So do not assign one constant chi across the entire ferromagnetic curve.
At strong enough fields, magnetisation approaches saturation; it cannot
increase without limit as a simple proportionality might suggest.
Some magnetisation can remain after the external field is removed.
The retained response is associated with magnetic memory.
A reverse field can be required to reduce the magnetisation to zero: that is
the idea behind coercivity.
Soft magnetic materials are relatively easy to magnetise and demagnetise,
useful in changing field cores.
Hard magnetic materials resist demagnetisation and suit permanent magnets.
Soft and hard here describe magnetic response, not how easily you scratch the
surface.
Iron, cobalt and nickel are standard ferromagnetic examples, under suitable
temperature conditions.
Heating a ferromagnet increases thermal disorder.
At its Curie temperature, spontaneous ferromagnetic ordering is lost.
Above that transition, the material becomes paramagnetic.
It does not become incapable of responding to a magnetic field.
That distinction is a favourite conceptual trap.
Cooling below the transition can restore ferromagnetic ordering, but does not
by itself guarantee the same macroscopic permanent magnetisation as before.
Domain arrangement and magnetic history still matter.
Also, do not extend the elementary chi equals C over T rule through this
transition.
Near a ferromagnetic transition, the temperature dependence is more subtle.
Let's finish with a separate linear material problem.
Internal H is one thousand amperes per meter, susceptibility is zero point
zero
one, and the material is isotropic and linear in the stated range.
First find magnetisation.
Ten amperes per meter, along H.
Next, B equals mu zero times one thousand and ten.
Taking mu zero approximately four pi times ten to the minus seven in SI units
gives about one point two six nine millitesla.
Without that material response, mu zero H would be about one point two five
seven millitesla.
The increase is only one percent.
Positive susceptibility alone does not prove ferromagnetism.
Classify by the response regime, its magnitude, microscopic ordering and
history.
Your final checklist is sign, direction, field gradient, absolute temperature
and model validity.
Those five checks turn a memorised table into usable physics.
